chapter_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
periods.activity_title: First Encounter with Minam's Mountain Journey

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp.111–115): teacher-led read-aloud of the narrative with new words.

time_bands.activity: Invite children to share what they know about mountains or a journey they have taken. Collect a few responses to build curiosity about the story.
Let us Read — read the narrative aloud (pp.111–115), pausing at key moments — Minam packing her bag, meeting the yaks, seeing snow for the first time — to maintain engagement.
Revisit the new words: Himalayas, Sherpa, journey, loads, memories, mighty. Write each on the board, say it aloud together, and ask children to locate it in the text.
Shared re-reading: pairs take turns reading a paragraph each aloud while the teacher circulates and gently corrects pronunciation.
Close by asking one or two children: what moment in the story surprised you most? Accept brief responses.

periods.teacher_notes: The narrative is rich with sensory detail — fresh mountain air, cool river water, musical Santoor notes — and pausing to let children visualise these moments deepens engagement. Watch that children do not stumble silently on 'Sherpa' or 'Himalayas'; model the pronunciation clearly before shared reading. New words can be revisited organically as they appear in the text rather than as a separate list.

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.116): six short-answer comprehension questions on the narrative.

homework.task_brief: Let us Think C (p.117): match five items from the story (favourite fruit, lunch place, mountain animals, tallest peak, rock-climbing animals).

time_bands.activity: Invite a child to retell the story in two or three sentences — where Minam went, what she saw, and how she felt at the end. This draws the narrative back into focus.
Let us Think A (p.116), questions 1–3: teacher reads each question aloud, gives pairs one minute to discuss quietly, then takes answers from the class with brief elaboration.

Let us Think A (p.116), questions 4–6: same paired-discuss-then-share routine; for question 6 (Minam's promise), encourage children to explain what 'protecting the mountains' might mean in their own words.
Teacher writes three or four answers on the board drawn from student responses; class votes on which best captures the story, giving reasons.
Introduce the homework matching task (p.117): read the two columns aloud together and ask children to attempt it at home.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the narrative together, children now have the story fresh and can find textual evidence for their answers. A common difficulty is question 6 — children may offer vague answers about 'loving nature'; prompt them to use Minam's own words from the story. Keep pairs mixed so stronger readers support emerging ones.

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
periods.activity_title: Discussing the Journey: Connecting to Our Own World

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (pp.116–117): three guided discussion prompts connecting Minam's journey to children's own experiences.

time_bands.activity: Recall that Minam learned about yaks, snow and the Himalayas from her grandfather on their walk together. Ask: who teaches you things outside the classroom? Gather a few quick answers to warm up.

Let us Think B (p.116), prompt 1: in small groups of three, children share a person in their family or community who has taught them something special and what they learned. Teacher circulates and listens.

Let us Think B (p.117), prompt 2: whole-class discussion — children name animals or things in their surroundings that help people, as yaks and mountain goats help mountain communities. Teacher builds a list on the board.

Let us Think B (p.117), prompt 3: partner talk — each child tells their partner one thing in nature near their home or school that should be protected and one thing they could do. Two or three pairs share with the class.
Brief close: the teacher summarises the thread — Minam's promise connects to the children's own promises. Ask children to hold that thought.

periods.teacher_notes: The three prompts move from personal memory (a family teacher) to observation (helpful animals nearby) to commitment (protecting nature); keep that arc gentle and unhurried. Children who struggle to identify a community teacher can be prompted with broader examples — an elder, a neighbour, a coach. Accept all sincere responses without ranking them.

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
periods.activity_title: Sentence Completion Game: Speaking in Turns

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (p.123): sentence completion game — groups alternate giving and completing sentence starters.

time_bands.activity: Demonstrate the game with two volunteers: the teacher offers 'On a bright summer morning, …' and a child completes it aloud. Swap — the child offers a starter and the teacher completes it. Show what a good starter sounds like.
Divide the class into Group A and Group B facing each other. Explain that each group will give a starter, the other will complete it, and they will alternate.

Let us Speak (p.123): run several rounds of the game. Encourage children to use the adventure and nature themes from Minam's journey as inspiration for their starters — mountains, animals, journeys, discoveries.
Pause the game and invite three or four children to share the most imaginative or surprising completion they heard. Brief class appreciation after each.
Whole-group reflection: what made a sentence starter interesting? What made a completion surprising or funny? Children respond freely.

periods.teacher_notes: This game builds spontaneous oral fluency; resist the urge to correct grammar mid-game — save corrections for after the round is over. Children who freeze on a starter can be reminded of events from the story: setting off on a journey, seeing an animal for the first time, reaching a hilltop. Keep the energy brisk so every child speaks at least once.

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
periods.activity_title: Story Words in Action: Fill-ins and Crossword

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.117): complete six sentences using key story words.
Let us Learn B (p.118): solve the mountain-themed crossword puzzle.

time_bands.activity: Write the six word-bank items on the board: Himalayas, Sherpa, journey, heavy loads, snowman, memories. Ask children to predict which word goes with the idea of 'Minam's grandfather's old job' before opening books.
Let us Learn A (p.117): children work independently to complete the six sentences. Teacher then reads each sentence aloud and cold-calls for the answer; the class echoes the completed sentence.
Transition: tell the class they will now use those same ideas in a crossword. Briefly show the grid and explain Across and Down.

Let us Learn B (p.118): children solve the crossword individually or in pairs. Teacher circulates, offering clue prompts — 'This word describes Minam's grandfather's role on the mountain' — rather than giving answers directly.
Check the crossword answers together by having volunteers call out each word while the class ticks their own grids. Clap for any child who got all seven.

periods.teacher_notes: The six fill-in words all appear in the narrative, so children who draw on the story have a strong advantage — encourage them to recall rather than guess. In the crossword, 'valley' and 'plateau' are the two words children are least likely to produce spontaneously; if most are stuck, offer the first letter as a prompt.

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (p.119): match six story words to their meanings.
Let us Learn D (p.119): match body-part words used to describe objects (foot, arm, heart, etc.).

time_bands.activity: Recall the phrase from the story: 'at the foot of the mighty Himalayas'. Ask children what 'foot' means here — is it a body part? Take two or three responses to surface the idea of figurative body-part words.
Let us Learn C (p.119): children read both columns and draw match lines individually. Review together — for each match, ask a child to use the word in an oral sentence about the story.
Bridge to the body-part task: write 'legs of the table', 'hands of the clock', 'neck of the bottle' on the board. Ask children to spot what these have in common.
Let us Learn D (p.119): pairs work through the five matching items. Encourage children to say the completed phrase aloud — 'the arm of the chair' — to feel whether it sounds right.
Invite children to invent one new body-part phrase not on the list (e.g. 'the back of the bus'). Accept playful suggestions; the class judges whether they work.

periods.teacher_notes: The body-part metaphor task (Let us Learn D) is playful but linguistically rich — children are discovering that English borrows human anatomy to name object parts. Keep the mood light and exploratory rather than corrective. The invented-phrase activity in the closing band is an open extension; do not worry if children produce unusual combinations, as long as they can explain the logic.

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
periods.activity_title: Geography Words: Dictionary Hunt and Labelling

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p.120): look up geography words in a dictionary, then label the mountain landscape diagram.

time_bands.activity: Ask children to name the geographical features they remember from Minam's journey — the river, the peaks, the snow. List their suggestions on the board.

Let us Write A (p.120): children look up each of the nine words (Plain, River, Valley, Summit, Foot, Slope, Plateau, Hill, Mountain range) in their dictionaries and write a brief meaning beside each word.
Quick meaning check: teacher reads each word and a child volunteers the meaning they found. Clarify any that are confused — particularly 'plateau' versus 'valley', and 'summit' versus 'peak'.
Children label the mountain landscape diagram on p.120 using the nine geography words. Teacher circulates, prompting careful placement — 'Is the river at the top or bottom of the mountain?'
Pairs swap books and check each other's labels. Teacher draws a simple sketch on the board and invites volunteers to call out where each label belongs; class confirms.

periods.teacher_notes: Dictionary use is genuinely practised here, not just listed — give children unhurried time to locate entries. A common confusion is placing 'foot' as a body-part word rather than recognising it as the base of a slope; a quick reminder of the phrase from the story ('at the foot of the Himalayas') usually resolves this. The diagram on p.120 is the visual anchor; keep the book open.

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
periods.activity_title: Conjunctions: Joining Sentences with and, but, or, because

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (pp.121–122): join ten sentence pairs using the correct conjunction from given choices.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'Minam was tired. She was happy.' Ask: can we join these with one word? Elicit 'but'. Then try 'She stayed home. She was not feeling well.' — draw out 'because'. Introduce the four conjunctions: and, or, but, because, with a brief meaning for each.

Model items 1 and 2 from Let us Write B (p.121) on the board, thinking aloud: 'She was hungry — and then what happened? OR is she choosing? BUT means something unexpected. BECAUSE gives a reason.' Show how to read the choices.
Let us Write B (pp.121–122): children complete items 3–10 independently in their notebooks, choosing from the bracketed options and writing the joined sentence in full.
Review answers together: teacher reads each original pair aloud, a child names their conjunction, and the class reads the joined sentence in chorus. Discuss any item where children disagree.
Oral extension: ask two or three children to make up their own pair of sentences and choose the right conjunction. Peers confirm or suggest an alternative.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common difficulty is distinguishing 'but' (contrast) from 'because' (reason) — items 7 and 8 on p.122 often catch children. A quick test: ask 'Does the second sentence give a reason or a surprise?' to help them decide. Writing the full joined sentence (not just the conjunction) is important; circulate to ensure children do not leave the answer as a single word.

periods.section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
periods.activity_title: Himalayan Animal Chart and Everest Explorer

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.124): choose a Himalayan animal or bird, create an annotated chart with habitat, adaptation, and survival details, and share with the class.
Let us Explore (p.124): find out and share who was the first woman to climb Mount Everest twice.

time_bands.activity: Recall that Minam saw yaks on her journey and learned how they help mountain communities. Ask: what other animals live in those cold, high places? List any the children name.

Let us Do (p.124): present the six animal and bird options (Snow Leopard, Himalayan Tahr, Red Panda, Himalayan Brown Bear, Blood Pheasant, Yak). Each child or pair chooses one. Explain the four headings their chart must cover: habitat, adaptation, life cycle and lifestyle, survival in harsh conditions.

Children plan and create their chart on a sheet of paper — drawing the animal, labelling key features, and writing one or two caption sentences under each heading. Teacher circulates, asking 'How does this animal stay warm?' or 'What does it eat?' to prompt thinking.
Three or four volunteers present their chart briefly to the class. After each, invite one question from the audience. Teacher highlights one interesting fact from each presentation.

Let us Explore (p.124): teacher tells the class that a woman climbed Mount Everest twice — the first ever to do so. Ask children to guess who she might be, then share the answer (Santosh Yadav) and invite children to find one more fact about her as a personal curiosity to follow up.

periods.teacher_notes: Since children may not have reference materials at hand, encourage them to draw on what they know from books, television, or conversations at home — the chart is an expression of their curiosity, not a research report. If library books are available, bring a few to the room. The Let us Explore prompt is brief and open-ended; it is designed to spark curiosity rather than demand a finished product in these minutes.
materials: Plain paper and coloured pencils for charts
Library books on Himalayan animals (if available)

items.source_section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
items.source_lo: Student recalls and explains story events and character actions using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Minam's Himalayan journey with her grandfather — yaks, snow, Everest, her promise.
items.item_stem: Read the statements below and mark each True or False.

options.text: Minam's grandfather was a former Sherpa who had worked in the Himalayas.
Minam and her grandfather had lunch on the snow-covered ground near a snowman.
Minam had never seen snow before she made a snowman with her grandfather.
Minam's grandfather pointed out Mount Everest as the world's second tallest mountain.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True. 2 — False: they stopped for lunch by a clear river, not on the snow. 3 — True. 4 — False: Grandfather pointed out Mount Everest as the world's tallest mountain.

items.source_section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
items.source_lo: Student recalls and explains story events and character actions using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Minam's Himalayan journey with her grandfather — yaks, snow, Everest, her promise.
items.item_stem: By the end of her journey, Minam made a special promise to her grandfather. What was her promise, and what do you think it tells us about how the journey changed her?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Minam promised to protect the mountains and share their magic with everyone she meets. This shows that the journey turned her from someone who had never seen snow into someone who felt responsible for the natural world around her.

items.source_section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
items.source_lo: Student connects a narrative's themes to personal experience and speaks in turn using a guided-conversation format as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Intergenerational learning, helpful animals, nature protection — drawn from Minam's mountain journey.
items.item_stem: In the story, Minam's grandfather teaches her about yaks, mountain goats, and the Himalayas during their walk. Listen to this question and choose the best answer: Why is it helpful to learn from an older family member or community elder when exploring a new place?

options.label: A
options.text: They can share knowledge and experience about the place that books may not have.

options.label: B
options.text: They always know the exact scientific names of every plant and animal.

options.label: C
options.text: They will carry all the heavy bags so children do not get tired.

options.label: D
options.text: They speak more loudly so everyone can hear the information clearly.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the child values formal scientific knowledge over lived experience and wisdom.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a literal reading that focuses on physical help rather than the knowledge-sharing the story demonstrates.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misses the meaning of the relationship; focuses on a superficial feature rather than the value of experiential knowledge.

items.source_section_title: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
items.source_lo: Student connects a narrative's themes to personal experience and speaks in turn using a guided-conversation format as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Intergenerational learning, helpful animals, nature protection — drawn from Minam's mountain journey.
items.item_stem: Minam promised to protect the mountains and share their magic with everyone she meets. Think of one thing in nature near your home or school that you feel should be protected. Speak about it: name it, explain why it matters, and say one thing you could do to keep it safe.

expected_elements: Names a specific natural feature or living thing.
Gives a reason why it matters to people or animals.

items.item_stem:
Fill in each blank with the correct conjunction from the box to join the two ideas. (and / but / because / or)
1. Minam was tired after the long walk _______ she was very happy.
2. Her grandfather pointed out Mount Everest _______ told her it was the world's tallest mountain.
3. They could rest by the river _______ they could climb higher to see the snow.
4. Minam made a snowman _______ she had never seen snow before.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Minam writing in your diary the evening after the mountain journey. Write three to four sentences about what you saw and how you felt. Use at least two conjunctions (and, but, or, because) in your writing.

expected_elements: Mentions at least one specific sight from the journey.
Uses at least two conjunctions correctly.
Expresses Minam's feelings in the child's own words.

Word | Meaning

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sherpa — Guides and helpers in mountain climbing; Yaks — Large, strong animals found in snowy mountains; Himalayas — The tallest mountain range in the world; Memories — Things we remember and cherish; Mighty — Very powerful or impressive.

Large, strong animals found in snowy mountains

items.item_stem: In the story, we read about Minam's village at the 'foot of the Himalayas'. Here, 'foot' is used like a body part to name a part of the mountain. Choose ONE of the body-part phrases below and say a sentence using it correctly: 'the neck of the bottle' — 'the arm of the chair' — 'the heart of the city'.

expected_elements: Chooses one of the three listed phrases.
Uses it in a complete, sensible sentence.
Shows understanding that the body-part word names an object part.

items.item_stem: Match each Himalayan animal or bird with one fact that describes it.
items.visual_stimulus:
Animal / Bird | Fact
Snow Leopard | A large mountain animal used for milk, wool, and carrying heavy loads
Red Panda | A guide and experienced climber who helps mountaineers in the Himalayas
Yak | A big wild cat with thick spotted fur that lives in snowy mountain regions
Sherpa | A small reddish animal that eats bamboo and lives in mountain forests
Blood Pheasant | A brightly coloured mountain bird found in the Himalayas

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Snow Leopard — A big wild cat with thick spotted fur that lives in snowy mountain regions; Red Panda — A small reddish animal that eats bamboo and lives in mountain forests; Yak — A large mountain animal used for milk, wool, and carrying heavy loads; Sherpa — A guide and experienced climber who helps mountaineers in the Himalayas; Blood Pheasant — A brightly coloured mountain bird found in the Himalayas.

answer_key.right: A big wild cat with thick spotted fur that lives in snowy mountain regions
A small reddish animal that eats bamboo and lives in mountain forests
A large mountain animal used for milk, wool, and carrying heavy loads
A guide and experienced climber who helps mountaineers in the Himalayas
A brightly coloured mountain bird found in the Himalayas

items.item_stem: Choose one animal from the story's world — the Snow Leopard, the Red Panda, or the Yak — and prepare a short spoken presentation about it. Tell the class: what the animal looks like, where it lives in the Himalayas, and one amazing thing it can do to survive in the cold.

expected_elements: Names and describes the chosen animal's appearance.
Shares one survival adaptation in own words.
